title: Symphonic Dances
hook: Rachmaninoff’s last work, written on Long Island in 1940, ends with the chant of death and a thank-you to God.

painting.title: The Dance of Life
painting.pairingNote: Couples dance by the sea on a moonlit summer night, watched by a young woman in white and an older one in black; life as a dance from youth to old age, like the Dances Rachmaninoff first called Noon, Twilight and Midnight.

facts: The Symphonic Dances were Rachmaninoff’s last major work, and the only one he wrote entirely in the United States. He composed them in the summer and autumn of 1940, mostly at Orchard Point, an estate in Centerport on Long Island, overlooking the Sound. He was 67, and had left Russia more than twenty years before.

He first called them *Fantastic Dances*, with the movements titled “Noon”, “Twilight” and “Midnight”. He dropped the titles before publication, but the idea of a day, or a life, moving towards night stays in the music.

He dedicated the work to Eugene Ormandy and the Philadelphia Orchestra, who gave the premiere on 3 January 1941. He also made a version for two pianos, and played the music through for the choreographer Michel Fokine, who wanted to make a ballet of it; Fokine’s death in 1942 ended the plan.

The music is full of memories: the theme of his First Symphony, a failure of 1897; the old chant of the dead, the [[dies-irae|Dies irae]]; and a chant of resurrection from his own *All-Night Vigil* of 1915. On the last page of the score he wrote: “I thank Thee, Lord”.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a march with a nostalgic song for saxophone (I), a ghostly waltz (II) and a midnight battle between death and resurrection (III).

movements.heading: Non allegro
movements.summary: “Not fast”: a march with sharp edges. Quiet pulsing in the strings, a little falling figure in the woodwinds, then heavy, hammered chords for the whole orchestra. In the middle the music slows and an alto saxophone, rare in a symphony orchestra, sings a long, nostalgic melody over the woodwinds alone. At the end the orchestra recalls, now in a glowing major key, the theme of his First Symphony.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: a three-note falling figure and stamping, staccato chords.

mainIdeas.name: The saxophone melody
mainIdeas.description: long, sad and Russian in feeling, over a soft bed of oboes, clarinets and cor anglais.

mainIdeas.name: The First Symphony theme
mainIdeas.description: heard only at the end, transformed from minor into major.

stops.hear: Soft, pulsing repeated notes in the strings; the woodwinds play a small falling figure
Loud, hammered chords from the whole orchestra
The figure is tossed around the orchestra, sharp and rhythmic
Everything slows; an alto saxophone sings a long, melancholy tune over quiet woodwinds, with no strings
The strings take up the melody and it swells
The pulsing and the hammered chords return
The music calms; a broad, warm melody unfolds in the major, with soft glittering sounds above it
stops.happening: The theme of the First Symphony, now in the major

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: A quiet, shimmering close

notice: Listen to the saxophone. Rachmaninoff writes the melody without any strings at all, so that its reedy, vocal sound stands out.

Listen to the theme at the end. In 1897 it belonged to the symphony whose disastrous premiere left him unable to compose for some three years; here, more than forty years later, it returns calm and in the major.

movements.heading: Andante con moto (Tempo di valse)
movements.summary: A [[waltz|waltz]], but a strange one. It starts hesitantly, with fragments and muted chords; a solo violin and then the woodwinds try out the tune. The metre keeps shifting and the tempo ebbs and flows, so that the dance never quite settles. It swells to a sweeping climax and then slips away, like dancers seen through a window at dusk.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: muted, stuttering chords, like a ghostly invitation to dance.

mainIdeas.name: The waltz tune
mainIdeas.description: a melancholy, sliding melody first for solo violin and woodwinds, then the strings.

stops.hear: Muted, stuttering chords in the brass, with silences between them
stops.happening: A dark invitation to the dance

stops.hear: A solo violin plays a short, wistful phrase
stops.happening: The waltz begins to take shape

stops.hear: The woodwinds take up a melancholy waltz tune
The strings take over, fuller and more passionate
The muted chords of the opening return
The waltz whirls up to its biggest climax, pulling and pushing the tempo

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The music thins out and vanishes

notice: Try to count the waltz in three. It keeps slipping: Rachmaninoff changes the metre and asks for [[rubato|rubato]], so the dance seems to stumble and recover.

movements.heading: Lento assai – Allegro vivace
movements.summary: The “Midnight” movement. After a slow, dark opening, a restless dance breaks out, haunted by the [[dies-irae|Dies irae]], the medieval chant of the Day of Judgement that runs through so much of Rachmaninoff’s music. A slow middle section brings a lamenting, falling figure in the strings and tolling bells. Then the dance returns, and a second chant enters: “Blessed art thou, O Lord” from his *All-Night Vigil*, a song of resurrection. Over it he wrote “Alliluya”. The two chants fight it out to the end.

mainIdeas.name: The *Dies irae*
mainIdeas.description: the chant of death, sometimes plain, sometimes hidden inside the dance.

mainIdeas.name: The resurrection chant
mainIdeas.description: a broad, solemn melody from the *All-Night Vigil*.

stops.hear: Slow, heavy chords, dark and uneasy
A fast, nervous dance starts up in the strings and woodwinds
A short, falling chant-like phrase keeps coming back in the dance
The music slows; the strings sing a lamenting, falling line; bells toll softly
The fast dance returns, wilder
A broad, solemn chant rises in the brass and woodwinds
stops.happening: “Blessed art thou, O Lord”: the resurrection chant, marked “Alliluya”

stops.hear: Both chants, death and resurrection, sound against each other at full force with all the percussion

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A last, crashing chord
stops.happening: The end of Rachmaninoff’s last work

notice: Listen for the *Dies irae*: four notes falling and rising in a small space. Rachmaninoff used it in many works; here it meets a chant of resurrection, and the music has to decide between them.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Jansons recorded the Dances with the St Petersburg Philharmonic in its own hall in September 1992, together with Rachmaninoff’s Third Symphony; on Spotify the Dances are tracks 4–6 of that album. The violin solos are played by Vladimir Ovcharek.

threads.title: A day that becomes a life
threads.body: Noon, twilight, midnight: the original titles are gone, but the three dances still move from bright energy through a fading waltz to the night.

threads.title: Old music remembered
threads.body: The First Symphony in movement I, the *All-Night Vigil* in movement III: in his last work Rachmaninoff looks back at his Russian past.

threads.title: Death and resurrection
threads.body: The *Dies irae* haunts the whole work; the last movement answers it with a chant of resurrection and a word of thanks on the final page.
